sentences.text: Jakapil was a small, armored dinosaur less than 1.5 meters long and weighing between 4.5 and 7 kilograms. It possessed a short, robust skull with only 11 pairs of leaf-shaped teeth in the lower jaw, lacking a dental cingulum. Its body was protected by at least five types of osteoderms, including large D-shaped plates on the neck sides and spine-like structures along its back.
This animal is remarkable for possessing a predentary bone, a feature absent or cartilaginous in other basal thyreophorans.

The holotype fossil of Jakapil was discovered in 2012 and excavated between 2014 and 2019/2020 from land owned by the Mariluan family. The genus name Jakapil comes from a Puelchean word meaning "shield bearer," while the species name kaniukura means "crest stone" in Mapudungun, referring to the animal's uniquely deep jaw.
Researchers suggest Jakapil processed tough plant material via mastication rather than shearing leaves, a hypothesis supported by high wear on its teeth.

Jakapil lived during the mid-Cretaceous, approximately 97 to 94 million years ago, in what is now South America. Fossil records place Jakapil in the Albian stage, between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago. It inhabited the Kokorkom desert, an ancient desert ecosystem with oases typical of the Mid-Cretaceous in western Gondwana.

Some researchers dispute Jakapil's classification as a thyreophoran, arguing it possesses unique features not found in other members of the group. A study concluded that Jakapil is likely an armored marginocephalian or a member of an unknown lineage of non-thyreophoran ornithischians. In 2024 analyses, Fonseca and colleagues suggested Jakapil could be the sister taxon to Eurypoda or the earliest member of Ankylosauria.
